entries.meaning: A person who spends time with someone, especially on a trip or in daily life. ---
examples: The dog has been her companion for ten years.
He hired a companion for his elderly mother.
My travel companions were both from Texas.

entries.meaning: A fellow member of a group, especially soldiers or political allies. ---
examples: He was buried beside his comrades.
Old comrades from the union came to the funeral.
She addressed the crowd as comrades.
entries.contrast: Americans say KAHM-rad; the British say KOM-rayd.

entries.meaning: A person of the same age or rank as someone else. ---
examples: Teenagers care most about their peers.
Peer pressure got him into trouble.
Her work is reviewed by peers before publication.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like pier, a walkway out over water.

entries.meaning: A friend, in casual American speech. ---
examples: He went fishing with his buddies.
My old army buddy called last night.
Hey, buddy, you dropped your wallet.

entries.meaning: A person who is rejected by their community. ---
examples: After the trial he was a social outcast.
The village treated them as outcasts.
She writes about outcasts and loners.

entries.meaning: An experienced person who advises and helps someone younger. ---
examples: Every new teacher is assigned a mentor.
He credits two mentors with his career.
She became a mentor to a dozen young lawyers.

entries.meaning: A person or company that pays for or vouches for someone or something. ---
examples: The team lost its main sponsor.
New immigrants often need a sponsor.
Several sponsors pulled out of the festival.

entries.meaning: Unity and mutual support among people who share a cause. ---
examples: The teachers marched in solidarity with the nurses.
There was little solidarity between the two unions.
They wore black as a show of solidarity.

entries.meaning: The act of working together toward the same goal. ---
examples: The project needs cooperation from three agencies.
Thank you for your cooperation.
There was no cooperation between the departments.

entries.meaning: An argument or disagreement, especially a formal one. ---
examples: The dispute went to arbitration.
Border disputes have troubled the region for decades.
They settled the dispute out of court.

entries.meaning: An agreement in which each side gives up part of what it wanted. ---
examples: They reached a compromise after six hours.
Marriage is full of small compromises.
Neither side would accept the compromise.

entries.meaning: Influence has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She has a lot of influence on the board.
His teacher was a good influence.
Her early influences were all jazz musicians.
His older brother was a bad influence on him.
She was the biggest influence on my writing.
Blues and gospel were early influences on the band.

senses.head: The power to affect how people think or act
examples: She has a lot of influence on the board.
His teacher was a good influence.
Her early influences were all jazz musicians.

senses.head: A person or thing that affects how someone behaves or develops
examples: His older brother was a bad influence on him.
She was the biggest influence on my writing.
Blues and gospel were early influences on the band.

entries.русский: влияние; человек (или фактор), влияющий на кого-л.

entries.meaning: The general opinion people hold about someone or something. ---
examples: The school has an excellent reputation.
One bad review can ruin a reputation.
He built his reputation over thirty years.

entries.meaning: The respect and admiration that a person or institution enjoys. ---
examples: The job carries a lot of prestige but little pay.
The award added to her prestige.
The university has lost some of its prestige.
entries.contrast: Ends in the zh sound of measure: pres-TEEZH.

entries.meaning: Talk about other people's private lives, often unkind or untrue. ---
examples: The office runs on gossip.
I heard some gossip about the new manager.
Don't believe every piece of gossip you hear.
entries.contrast: Uncountable — say a piece of gossip, not a gossip.

entries.meaning: Hospitality has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Southern hospitality is not a myth.
Thank you for your hospitality this weekend.
She works in the hospitality industry.

The college offers a two-year degree in hospitality.
Hospitality was the hardest-hit industry during the shutdown.

senses.head: Friendly, generous treatment of guests
examples: Southern hospitality is not a myth.
Thank you for your hospitality this weekend.
She works in the hospitality industry.

senses.head: The business of running hotels, restaurants, and other places that serve guests
examples: She has worked in hospitality since she was nineteen.
The college offers a two-year degree in hospitality.
Hospitality was the hardest-hit industry during the shutdown.

entries.русский: гостеприимство; гостиничный и ресторанный бизнес, индустрия гостеприимства

entries.meaning: The set of rules for polite behavior in a society or a profession. ---
examples: Business etiquette differs from country to country.
It's a breach of etiquette to arrive early.
Nobody taught him basic table etiquette.
entries.contrast: From French: most Americans say ET-ih-kut, though ET-ih-ket is also heard.

entries.meaning: A custom or belief passed down within a family or a society. ---
examples: Fireworks on the Fourth are an American tradition.
The family has its own holiday traditions.
Every school here has a homecoming tradition.

entries.meaning: Custom has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Shaking hands is an old custom.
Local customs vary from valley to valley.
It is the custom here to bring a dish.
Throwing rice at the couple is an old custom.
Wedding customs differ a lot from region to region.
It's the custom here to bring food to a grieving family.

senses.head: A way of behaving that is usual among a particular group of people
examples: Shaking hands is an old custom.
Local customs vary from valley to valley.
It is the custom here to bring a dish.

senses.head: A way of doing something that a group of people has followed for a long time
examples: Throwing rice at the couple is an old custom.
Wedding customs differ a lot from region to region.
It's the custom here to bring food to a grieving family.

entries.contrast: The plural customs also names the border office that inspects luggage.

entries.meaning: The traditions, buildings, and culture handed down from earlier generations. ---
examples: She's proud of her Mexican heritage.
The town protects its architectural heritage.
Music is part of our national heritage.

entries.meaning: A standard of behavior that is usual or expected in a group. ---
examples: Social norms change slowly.
Working from home has become the norm.
He ignored every norm of polite behavior.

entries.meaning: Inequality has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Income inequality has grown for decades.
The report lists inequalities in health care.
Inequality between the two districts is obvious.
He wrote the inequality x > 5 on the board.
Solve the inequality and graph it on a number line.
The homework was ten inequalities to solve.

senses.head: An unfair difference between groups in wealth, rights, or opportunity
examples: Income inequality has grown for decades.
The report lists inequalities in health care.
Inequality between the two districts is obvious.

senses.head: In mathematics, a statement that one quantity is larger or smaller than another
examples: He wrote the inequality x > 5 on the board.
Solve the inequality and graph it on a number line.
The homework was ten inequalities to solve.

entries.meaning: An unfair act, or the condition of being treated unfairly. ---
examples: She spent her life fighting injustice.
The book lists the injustices of that era.
It would be an injustice to blame him.

entries.meaning: The belief that one race is better than another, and unfair treatment based on it. ---
examples: The team was accused of racism.
Racism shaped where people were allowed to buy homes.
He spoke openly about the racism he faced.

entries.meaning: Unfair treatment of people, usually women, because of their sex. ---
examples: Sexism in the industry is still common.
She called out the casual sexism in the meeting.
The policy was struck down as plain sexism.

entries.meaning: The forced separation of groups of people, especially by race. ---
examples: Segregation in schools was ruled unconstitutional.
He grew up under legal segregation.
Housing segregation persists in many cities.

entries.meaning: The process of bringing separated groups together as equals. ---
examples: Integration of the schools took years.
The city has a long history of racial integration.
Integration into a new country is never easy.

entries.meaning: Work aimed at bringing about political or social change. ---
examples: Her activism started in college.
Online activism rarely changes laws by itself.
He gave up law for full-time activism.

entries.meaning: The giving of money and effort to help other people. ---
examples: He turned to philanthropy after selling the company.
American philanthropy funds many museums.
Her philanthropy focused on rural schools.
entries.contrast: Ph is said like f, and the stress falls on the second syllable: fuh-LAN-thruh-pee.

entries.meaning: The condition of having no job, or the number of people without one. ---
examples: Unemployment fell to four percent.
He's been collecting unemployment since March.
Youth unemployment is the real problem.

entries.meaning: The condition of having nowhere to live. ---
examples: The city declared an emergency over homelessness.
Homelessness rose sharply after the rents went up.
Nobody has solved homelessness here.

entries.meaning: The change in a poor neighborhood as wealthier people move in and prices rise. ---
examples: Gentrification pushed most of the old families out.
The new coffee shops are a sign of gentrification.
Residents organized against gentrification.

entries.meaning: A person who owns the house they live in. ---
examples: Homeowners pay the property tax.
As a new homeowner, she's always fixing something.
The storm left thousands of homeowners without insurance.

entries.meaning: All the people who work for a company or in a country. ---
examples: The company cut its workforce by a third.
Women entered the workforce in huge numbers.
Both workforces were unionized.

entries.meaning: Labor has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The price includes parts and labor.
Organized labor backed the candidate.
Farms here depend on seasonal labor.
She went into labor just after midnight.
Labor lasted almost fourteen hours.
He drove her to the hospital as soon as labor started.

senses.head: Work, especially hard physical work, or the workers who do it
examples: The price includes parts and labor.
Organized labor backed the candidate.
Farms here depend on seasonal labor.

senses.head: The process of giving birth, from the first contractions onward
examples: She went into labor just after midnight.
Labor lasted almost fourteen hours.
He drove her to the hospital as soon as labor started.

entries.русский: труд; рабочая сила; роды, родовые схватки
entries.contrast: Americans write labor; the British write labour.

entries.meaning: A young person learning a trade by working under a skilled worker. ---
examples: He started as an apprentice electrician.
The shop takes two apprentices a year.
Apprentices earn less while they train.

entries.meaning: The ideas and tastes shared by most people in a society. ---
examples: The band never broke into the mainstream.
Those views are now part of the mainstream.
Mainstream opinion has shifted a lot.

entries.meaning: Celebrity has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Three celebrities showed up for the benefit.
He became a minor celebrity overnight.
Celebrities get treated differently everywhere.
The book brought her sudden celebrity.
He was never comfortable with his new celebrity.
Celebrity did not make the job any easier.

senses.head: A famous person, especially in entertainment or sports
examples: Three celebrities showed up for the benefit.
He became a minor celebrity overnight.
Celebrities get treated differently everywhere.

senses.head: The state of being famous
examples: The book brought her sudden celebrity.
He was never comfortable with his new celebrity.
Celebrity did not make the job any easier.

entries.meaning: The state of being known by many people. ---
examples: Fame came late in his career.
She never wanted fame, only the work.
The book brought him worldwide fame.

entries.meaning: One person, considered separately from a group. ---
examples: The law protects the rights of the individual.
Several individuals were named in the report.
He's a strange individual, but harmless.

entries.meaning: Human beings in general, or a nation sharing a language and culture. ---
examples: A lot of people showed up.
The indigenous peoples of the Northwest fished for salmon.
They are a proud people with a long history.
entries.contrast: People is the everyday plural of person; the form peoples means nations or ethnic groups.

entries.meaning: A home where children without parents are raised. ---
examples: She was adopted from an orphanage at four.
The state closed its last orphanages in the seventies.
He grew up in a church orphanage.

entries.meaning: Protection from weather or danger, or a building that provides it. ---
examples: The family took shelter in the basement.
The city runs three homeless shelters.
We adopted a dog from the shelter.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: Uncountable as protection (to take shelter); countable as a building (two shelters).

entries.meaning: Care provided during the day for young children while their parents work. ---
examples: Both kids are in daycare now.
Daycare costs more than her rent.
The company opened a daycare center on site.
entries.русский: ясли, детский сад; присмотр за детьми
entries.contrast: Americans say daycare; the British say nursery.

entries.meaning: Reunion has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Our twentieth high school reunion is next fall.
Family reunions fill the campground every July.

Our twentieth high school reunion is in October.

senses.head: A social event where people who have not met in a long time come together
examples: Our twentieth high school reunion is next fall.
Family reunions fill the campground every July.
He skipped the reunion on purpose.

senses.head: A gathering of people who have not seen each other for a long time
examples: Our twentieth high school reunion is in October.
The family reunion draws about sixty people.
They've held reunions at the same lake since 1978.

entries.meaning: An event held to collect money for a cause, or a person who organizes one.
examples: The school held a bake sale as a fundraiser.
